analysis.one_liner: Directs EPA to set water pollution limits for PFAS chemicals and help treatment plants comply.
analysis.headline: The bill to set federal water limits for PFAS chemicals never got a committee vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: PFAS are man-made 'forever chemicals' found in nonstick cookware, waterproof clothing, firefighting foam, and industrial waste, and they have been linked to serious health problems. This bill would require the EPA to study which industries discharge PFAS into water, set legal discharge limits and water quality standards for them, and give public treatment plants up to $100,000 each in federal grants to filter PFAS out. It never received a vote in the House committee it was assigned to, and died when that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People who drink from or fish in waters contaminated by PFAS discharges — especially residents of New Hampshire, Michigan, and other communities near PFAS sources — plus publicly owned treatment plants that would get federal grants to install pretreatment technology.

how_it_helps.text: Requires EPA to review PFAS discharges from industrial sources and set enforceable effluent limits and pretreatment standards for covered substances like PFOA and PFOS.
Requires EPA to publish human-health water quality criteria for PFAS within two years of enactment.
Authorizes $100 million per year through 2025 in grants to publicly owned treatment works to help them implement PFAS pretreatment standards.

analysis.who_pays: Industrial facilities that discharge PFAS into water — including chemical makers, pulp and paper producers, and textile mills — would face new compliance costs, and taxpayers would fund the $100 million-per-year grant program.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs for industrial dischargers such as chemical manufacturers and textile mills could raise production costs, though the bill phases in limits over four years.
The bill relies on EPA rulemaking processes that can be slow and subject to revision, so limits might not take effect quickly even if enacted.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health and drinking-water benefits of limiting PFAS discharges likely outweigh the compliance costs, especially given growing evidence of PFAS harm, but the grant program adds federal spending.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and never received a vote before the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced in January 2020 and referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure.
Referred to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment six days later.
No further action was taken, and the bill died at the end of the 116th Congress without a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Industries that discharge PFAS into water — chemical manufacturers, textile mills, and pulp and paper plants — avoided new federal discharge limits, while communities with PFAS-contaminated water got no federal standards or funding from this bill.

for.name: Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick
for.what_they_did: Signed on as an original cosponsor.

against.name: House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill — no hearing or markup on record — before Congress ended.

against.name: PFAS-discharging industries
against.role: Chemical manufacturers, textile mills, pulp and paper producers
against.what_they_did: Would have faced new effluent limits; the general chemical and manufacturing lobby opposed PFAS regulation.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship (13 Democrats and 1 Republican), and no recorded vote or opposition ever occurred.

industries.note: The bill would have required EPA to set effluent limits for PFAS discharges from chemical, textile, and pulp/paper facilities. Those industries bore the compliance cost.
Treatment plants would receive up to $100,000 each in federal grants to implement PFAS pretreatment standards.
